extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (MIT or equivalent) interested in an introduction to representation theory
extracted.subtask_description: Syllabus for an undergraduate-level course introducing representation theory of groups, Lie algebras, and associative algebras, listing topics, prerequisites, textbooks, meeting times, and grading policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course goal / level
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of this course is to give an undergraduate-level introduction to representation theory (of groups, Lie algebras, and associative algebras). Representation theory is an area of mathematics which, roughly speaking, studies symmetry in linear spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets expectation of undergraduate-level depth and scope (introductory treatment across groups, Lie algebras, associative algebras).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics to be covered / mastered
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive list of topics including: basic objects and notions (associative algebras, algebras by generators and relations, group algebras, quivers and path algebras, Lie algebras and enveloping algebras, representations, irreducible and indecomposable representations, Schur’s lemma, representations of sl(2)); general results (density theorem, representations of finite dimensional algebras, semisimple algebras, characters, Jordan–Hölder and Krull–Schmidt theorems, extensions); representations of finite groups (Maschke’s theorem, sum of squares formula, duals and tensor products, orthogonality of characters and matrix elements, character tables, unitary representations, computation of tensor product and restriction multiplicities, applications); further finite-group results (Frobenius–Schur indicator, Frobenius determinant, algebraic integers and Frobenius divisibility theorem, Burnside’s theorem, induced representations, Mackey formula, Frobenius reciprocity, representations of GL(2, F_q), symmetric and general linear groups, Schur–Weyl duality, invariant theory); representations of quivers (indecomposables of types A1, A2, A3, D4, triple of subspaces problem, Gabriel’s theorem, proof techniques including root systems and reflection functors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllabus enumerates concrete theorems, examples, and specific classes of objects that students are expected to learn; mastery of these topics constitutes the course content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites / required background
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerequisites are the standard algebra sequences Algebra I and II (18.701, 18.702) or Linear Algebra and Modern Algebra (18.700, 18.703).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further explanation: 'This means that to understand this course, it is necessary and sufficient to have a strong background in linear algebra and a decent understanding of basic algebraic structures, such as groups, rings, and fields.' Use this as the minimum competence threshold for enrolling or attempting course work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbooks and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the lecture notes, the course will use the beginning part of: Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course (Grad. Texts in Math. Vol. 129, Springer, 1991) and Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups (Grad. Texts in Math. Vol. 42, Springer-Verlag, 1977).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecture notes are primary; the listed texts are recommended supplemental references (beginning parts). ISBNs are provided for locating editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectures: meeting times and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures meet 2 sessions per week, 1.5 hours per session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistical constraint on contact hours and scheduling; implies expected attendance/participation opportunities but does not state an explicit attendance policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework schedule / submission cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Homeworks will be assigned every Thursday and due the following Thursday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular weekly homework cadence; students should plan weekly work and submission. The syllabus explicitly ties homework frequency to course pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework weight and pass requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Homeworks are 75% of the grade. 'To pass the course, it will be required to solve homework assignments which will be assigned every Thursday and due the following Thursday.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework performance is the primary assessment component and is mandatory for passing; implies substantial ongoing evaluation based on homework correctness and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration policy for homework
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ok to collaborate on homework if you creatively participate in solving it and understand what you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits collaboration but requires individual understanding and meaningful contribution; use this as the standard for acceptable collaborative practice (i.e., do not copy solutions you cannot explain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-home final assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: There will be a take-home final assignment at the end of the term which will weigh 25% of the grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final assessment is a take-home project/assignment rather than an in-person exam; constitutes a quarter of the final grade and likely tests cumulative understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment breakdown (activities percentages)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit grade composition — use these percentages to compute final course grade. No other graded components (e.g., participation, quizzes) are listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of hands-on exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllabus states 'there will be many hands-on exercises illustrating the course.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates pedagogical emphasis on worked examples and practice; students are expected to engage with and learn from practical exercises in addition to theoretical proofs.
